doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Diversity in booking and the Kenton reunions
summary: Poston describes taking diversity into account and addressing the lack of Black and female musicians in Kenton events.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What is the — is there any racial issues these days in booking concerts and diversity that you take into account with the productions that you manage?

Yes. I make sure, and I always have, even years ago before it was maybe as necessary even as it is today, but I’m always very conscious of those things and I try to take into account how what we’re doing is going to be perceived and so if we’re doing some kind of a historical event that doesn’t — maybe that doesn’t have the diversity for natural reasons or for reasons that, for whatever reasons that it can’t, I’m always aware enough of it to be able to discuss it or explain it or put it in the right perspective. But in this day and age, especially at the radio station, we’re on a college campus of course and as you know that’s a very, very important item right now — diversity is something that everyone is concerned about on every level at the college. And so everyone who works there and everyone who is in certain positions, even with us at the radio station, are expected, I’m sure, I mean no one comes out really and says it that way but I know we’re expected to approach what we do with all things considered. Now that doesn’t mean that you can always be all inclusive but it means that when you can you should be and you should make attempts maybe, and what we do is we make attempts to design certain things that open the door to specifically have that be a point of what we’re doing is to do things that represent a diversity whether it’s a racial diversity or other.
Yeah, I know what you mean. I do a —
We’ve been real careful with that.

And I don’t mean careful from the standpoint of you know trying to get by with that, it’s not that at all, it’s that we just try to make sure that we’re doing things — taking everything into consideration and doing things the right way.

And I’ve always kind of wanted to do that. I’ve always tried to do things — what I — in my mind at least is the right way. You know it was — I mean obviously, and again I keep going back to the Kenton thing but that’s just ‘cause that was kind of the one that established these things. If you’re going to do a Stan Kenton reunion you’re going to be very short on African-American musicians, you’re going to be very short on female musicians. Now there are some, and we include them, as far as female musicians I mean you know Mary Fettig’s been at a number of the events but you know Mary Fettig off the top of my head is about the only one I can think of that was a female musician that actually played in the Stan Kenton Orchestra. There are black musicians who were in the Kenton orchestra through the years, but not very many, and that’s where you get a lot of the racial things being written about someone like a Stan Kenton and so on and so forth with that. But again we try to, when we’ve done the Kenton things we’ve tried to address that, not to hide from it but to try to address it so that it’s presented in a way. Not presented necessarily — because I don’t pretend to be able to read anybody’s mind as to why this happened or didn’t happen, but here’s how it happened. Here’s historically what happened. And you know, so —

It does make sense. We have a kind of event here every year that I organize and sometimes it’s much like a jazz party where I call one person and I say, “Bring a band. Bring whoever you would like.” What I don’t say or have a hard time saying is: it would be a plus if it was a diverse quintet and I find that hard to say.

It’s hard ‘cause you can’t — you know it’s hard to tell the musicians, you know, to change whatever the make-up of the group is or whatever. But it’s yeah — and I understand it and it’s something important and I understand that it’s important but again it’s just one of those things that I don’t think there’s any right way or wrong way to approach it. I think it’s just a case by case basis for us as to whatever we’re doing, whatever we’re focused on and how we can best address things the right way and be inclusive, you know, when we can. And we do that a lot now. And again, I don’t ever like doing things for the wrong reasons. I mean I don’t like being inclusive ‘cause you feel like you have to, I like to do it because there’s a valid reason to do it. And so we try to, we try to still maintain a certain level of accomplishing what we set out to accomplish and do it the best way that we can.
